title: Battery Health Diagnostics & Replacement
contentStatus: PROPOSED title/content, pending DiFacto confirmation. Builds on confirmed LFP battery specs from L2-M3 (CDD-sourced). Specific diagnostic thresholds and replacement procedures pending DiFacto engineering documentation.

sections.title: From Awareness to Diagnosis
learningObjectives: Recall the battery fundamentals covered at L2
Understand the deeper diagnostic responsibility at Technician level
sections.content: L2-M3 covered battery awareness - LFP chemistry, confirmed runtime and charging specs, and recognizing when something seems off. This module goes deeper: actually diagnosing battery health issues and determining when a battery needs replacement rather than continued monitoring.

sections.title: How Battery Health Degrades Over Time
learningObjectives: Understand the general concept of battery capacity degradation
Recognize this as a normal, expected process rather than a fault
sections.content: All rechargeable batteries, including MoRo's LFP batteries, lose some capacity over repeated charge cycles - this is normal degradation, not a defect. The practical question for a Technician isn't whether degradation is happening (it always is, gradually) but whether it's progressing at an expected rate or faster than normal, and at what point remaining capacity no longer meets operational needs.

keyTerms.note: MoRo's battery chemistry, chosen for thermal stability and long cycle life — covered in detail in L2-M3.
The gradual, expected loss of a battery's maximum charge capacity over repeated use cycles.

sections.title: Diagnostic Indicators of Battery Issues
learningObjectives: Understand general categories of battery-related diagnostic signals
Distinguish normal aging from an abnormal issue
sections.content: Diagnostic signals worth tracking include charge time (taking meaningfully longer than expected), runtime per charge (shorter than the unit's typical pattern), and charging behavior (failing to reach full charge, or charging unevenly). A gradual, consistent decline across these metrics usually reflects normal aging; a sudden change is more likely to indicate an actual fault.

sections.title: Using the Diagnostic Interface for Battery Data
learningObjectives: Understand how the diagnostic interface (from L3A-M5) applies specifically to battery health
Know the general type of data available for battery diagnosis
sections.content: The diagnostic interface exposes battery-specific data beyond what the operator-level dashboard shows - detailed charge cycle history, temperature behavior during charging, and cell-level data where available. Specific screens and data points for battery diagnostics will be confirmed against DiFacto's technician documentation.

sections.title: Deciding on Replacement
learningObjectives: Understand the general criteria for recommending battery replacement
Recognize this as a judgment call informed by data, not a fixed rule alone
sections.content: Replacement decisions generally weigh remaining capacity against operational need - a battery that's degraded but still comfortably covers a unit's actual daily runtime requirement may not need replacement yet, even if it's below its original rated capacity. Specific replacement thresholds will be confirmed against DiFacto's guidance, but the underlying principle is assessing fitness for actual use, not just comparing against original spec.

sections.title: Safe Battery Handling
learningObjectives: Understand general safety considerations specific to battery handling
Recognize when battery work falls within Technician scope versus requiring escalation
sections.content: LFP batteries are generally considered safer than many other lithium chemistries, but battery handling still requires care - following proper lockout/tagout before any physical battery work, and recognizing signs (physical damage, unusual heat, swelling) that indicate a situation beyond routine replacement and requiring immediate escalation rather than continued handling.

questions.question: Is battery capacity degradation over time a sign of a defect?
options: Yes, any degradation indicates a faulty battery
No - gradual degradation over charge cycles is normal and expected
questions.feedback: Correct. Gradual capacity loss is a normal, expected characteristic of rechargeable batteries.

questions.question: What pattern of change is more likely to indicate an actual fault versus normal aging?
options: A sudden change in charging or runtime behavior
questions.feedback: Correct. Sudden changes are more indicative of an actual issue than gradual, expected aging.

questions.question: What does the diagnostic interface provide for battery health beyond the operator dashboard?
options: Detailed charge cycle history, temperature behavior, and cell-level data where available
questions.feedback: Correct. The diagnostic interface exposes deeper battery data for technician-level assessment.

questions.question: What should a replacement decision primarily weigh?
options: Only the battery's age in months
Remaining capacity against the unit's actual operational runtime need
Replacement should happen on a fixed schedule regardless of condition
questions.feedback: Correct. Fitness for actual operational use matters more than comparison to original spec alone.

questions.question: What should prompt immediate escalation rather than routine battery handling?
options: Signs like physical damage, unusual heat, or swelling
questions.feedback: Correct. Physical damage, unusual heat, or swelling indicate a situation requiring escalation, not routine handling.
